design_detail: Cochrane systematic review with meta-analysis (update of the 2001 review CD003021; RevMan, fixed-effect Mantel-Haenszel risk ratios and inverse-variance mean differences, random-effects standardized mean difference for withdrawal symptoms) of randomized and controlled clinical trials of medicines, alone or with psychosocial treatment, against placebo or psychosocial treatment alone, in people with amphetamine withdrawal. 'Amphetamines' in the review means amphetamine, dextroamphetamine and methamphetamine. Searches to 1 May 2008. Four randomized placebo-controlled trials (125 participants) were included: two of amineptine (Jittiwutikan 1997; Srisurapanont 1999b) and two of mirtazapine (Kongsakon 2005; Cruickshank 2008).
can_establish: Whether, in the four small placebo-controlled trials available up to May 2008, amineptine or mirtazapine changed treatment drop-out, clinician-rated global state, withdrawal symptoms or craving by the end of treatment in people with amphetamine withdrawal or dependence, and how far the trials can be trusted by the review's own risk-of-bias judgments.
cannot_establish: Whether any medicine eases the comedown of people who use amphetamines without dependence (every participant had a DSM-IV diagnosis and was in a treatment centre, probation facility or clinic); whether medicines never trialled (sleeping pills, other antidepressants, supplements) help; adverse effects (planned as a primary outcome, never reported); effects beyond the end of treatment; and, with 125 participants in all and at most 74 in any pooled analysis, whether a small or moderate benefit on withdrawal symptoms has been missed.

sample.recruitment: Three trials in Thailand (two among inpatients of a drug-dependence treatment centre, Jittiwutikan 1997 and Srisurapanont 1999b; one among detainees of a probation facility, Kongsakon 2005) and one in Australia (two public inner-city drug and alcohol outpatient clinics, Cruickshank 2008) (Results › Treatment setting; Characteristics of included studies).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: randomized or controlled clinical trials of any medicine, alone or with psychosocial treatment, against placebo or psychosocial treatment alone, in people with amphetamine withdrawal diagnosed by any criteria; samples withdrawing from several substances only if amphetamine data were separate or more than half had amphetamine withdrawal; studies with attrition of 50% or more excluded. Excluded at full text (five studies, reasons tabulated): a bupropion case report (Chan-Ob 2001), an open reboxetine case series (Cox 2004), a lisuride trial with mostly cocaine-dependent participants (Gillin 1994), an observational natural-history study of methamphetamine withdrawal (McGregor 2005) and a non-randomized comparison of mirtazapine and modafinil with treatment as usual (McGregor 2008a).
sample.demographics: Mostly young men (110 men, 15 women). Amineptine trials: inpatients meeting DSM-IV criteria for amphetamine withdrawal (Srisurapanont 1999b also required an Amphetamine Withdrawal Questionnaire score of 10 or more), mean ages 18.5 and 19.6 years, amphetamine use histories of about two years. Kongsakon 2005: 20 men with DSM-IV amphetamine dependence, mean age 24.3. Cruickshank 2008: 31 adults (20 men, 11 women) with DSM-IV amphetamine dependence and recent use of amphetamine or methamphetamine, mean age 31 (Results › Participant characteristics; Characteristics of included studies).
sample.attrition: Drop-out is itself the first outcome. Three trials analysed by last observation carried forward on an intention-to-treat basis and one had balanced drop-out across arms; the review assigned people lost to follow-up to the worst outcome for dichotomous data (Methods › Data synthesis; Results › Incomplete outcome data).
sample.selection_effects: Treatment-seeking or compelled samples (inpatient units, probation) dominated by young Thai men; nobody using amphetamines occasionally or outside treatment. Searches covered CENTRAL, MEDLINE, PsycINFO and CINAHL to May 2008 without language limits, plus reference lists, trial registers and conference proceedings; EMBASE was searched only for the original review (to December 2000). In the update one author screened titles and abstracts alone.

exposure.measurement: DSM-IV amphetamine withdrawal (two amineptine trials) or DSM-IV amphetamine dependence with recent use (two mirtazapine trials), as diagnosed by the trial investigators; the medicines were the randomized exposure.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as reported by the review: amineptine 300 mg a day by mouth (two 100 mg capsules after breakfast and one after lunch; dose titrated over the first 5 days in Jittiwutikan 1997), with occasional low-dose lorazepam allowed for moderate to severe anxiety or insomnia in both amineptine trials; mirtazapine 15 to 60 mg a day titrated by clinical response from 15 mg (Kongsakon 2005), or 15 mg at night for 2 nights then 30 mg at night for 12 nights with narrative-therapy counselling offered to both arms (Cruickshank 2008). Every trial lasted 14 days; outcomes were taken at the end of the 14-day medication period. Treatment began soon after admission: mean time since last amphetamine use about 53 to 58 hours in the amineptine trials; use within the previous 72 hours required in Cruickshank 2008.
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported in the review. Lorazepam co-medication was allowed in both amineptine trials, which could blunt differences in anxiety, sleep and global state between arms.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Participants were in early abstinence during treatment; how abstinence was verified in each trial is not described in the review.

comparison.controls: Placebo in all four trials (66 participants).
comparison.matching: Randomization. Sequence generation judged at low risk of bias in three trials (coin-tossing block randomization; pharmacist-run computer randomization) and unclear in one; allocation concealment low risk in one trial (Cruickshank 2008) and unclear in three (review's own judgments).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to randomized comparisons; the review does not report whether arms were balanced at baseline in each trial.

outcomes.instruments: Drop-out (did not complete the trial); global state by the Clinical Global Impression (two amineptine trials) or the Brief Symptom Inventory Global Severity Index (Cruickshank 2008); withdrawal symptoms by the Amphetamine Withdrawal Questionnaire (10 items, Srisurapanont 1999b; Kongsakon 2005 reported only medians) or the Amphetamine Cessation Symptoms Assessment (16 items, Cruickshank 2008); craving by the craving score of the Questionnaire for Evaluating Cocaine Craving and Related Responses (Jittiwutikan 1997). Adverse events, adherence and deaths were planned outcomes but no data on them are reported.
outcomes.validity_norms: The review accepted only scales published in a scientific journal. The craving instrument was developed for cocaine; the Amphetamine Cessation Symptoms Assessment adapts items from a cocaine scale.
outcomes.operationalization: Withdrawal severity as symptom-scale totals at the end of 14 days; global state as clinician-rated severity; no definition of a clinically important change.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Four outcomes were analysed, each overall and by medicine (10 rows in the data table).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Review's judgments for subjective outcomes: low risk in Cruickshank 2008 (clinical staff, research staff and participants blinded), unclear in the other three (assessor blinding not specified, or no blinding method described). Drop-out was judged unlikely to be influenced by blinding.

analysis.effect_sizes: Any medicine against placebo, drop-out: RR 0.52 (95% CI 0.29 to 0.94), 4 trials, 125 participants, I2 45%, p = 0.14 for heterogeneity; amineptine RR 0.21 (0.07 to 0.69), 2 trials, 74; mirtazapine RR 0.98 (0.49 to 1.97), 2 trials, 51. Global state (higher is worse): amineptine MD -0.49 (-0.80 to -0.17), 2 trials, 72; mirtazapine MD 0.30 (-0.22 to 0.82), 1 trial, 31; the data table also pools all three as MD -0.27 (-0.54 to -0.01), 103 participants, although the text says no combined result was calculated (I2 69%, p = 0.04). Withdrawal symptoms: SMD -0.08 (-0.54 to 0.38), 2 trials, 74 (amineptine -0.26, -0.86 to 0.34, 43 participants; mirtazapine 0.17, -0.54 to 0.89, 31). Craving (higher is less craving): amineptine MD 0.43 (-1.23 to 2.09), 1 trial, 29. Absolute numbers of drop-outs per arm are given only in the forest plots, which are images.
analysis.covariates: None (randomized comparisons). A sensitivity analysis on mixed-substance samples was planned; no included trial needed it.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Cochrane protocol published in Issue 2, 2001 (review first published Issue 4, 2001; this update 2009, with conclusions changed). The update changed the risk-of-bias method to the 2008 Cochrane Handbook and says so. Planned outcomes (adverse events as a primary outcome; adherence; deaths; medium- and long-term follow-up) are not reported, and the number needed to treat that the methods say was calculated appears nowhere.
analysis.selective_reporting: Adverse events, listed as a primary outcome, are not reported for any trial. Kongsakon 2005's withdrawal-symptom result (medians, reported as favouring mirtazapine) could not be pooled and is given only in words.
analysis.power: Not addressed. 125 participants in all; the withdrawal-symptom estimate rests on 74 people in two trials of two different medicines, and the craving estimate on 29.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In four small trials (125 people), neither amineptine nor mirtazapine reduced withdrawal symptoms compared with placebo (SMD -0.08, -0.54 to 0.38; 74 people) and amineptine did not reduce craving (29 people). Amineptine reduced drop-out (RR 0.21, 0.07 to 0.69) and improved clinician-rated global state (MD -0.49) in two trials from one Thai group; mirtazapine showed no benefit on drop-out or global state in the one trial with usable data, while a second trial reported fewer withdrawal symptoms in medians that could not be pooled.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that "No medication is effective for treatment of amphetamine withdrawal"; the implications for practice say more carefully that there is no evidence to guide the choice of medicine. Gaps: (1) the abstract's wording turns an absence of evidence into evidence of absence, although the withdrawal-symptom interval includes a moderate benefit; (2) the abstract says one trial suggested mirtazapine may reduce hyperarousal and anxiety symptoms, a detail not shown in the review's results; (3) the review's own risk-of-bias judgments (unclear allocation concealment and assessor blinding in three of four trials) are not used to temper the amineptine findings. Otherwise the review is restrained and states that the evidence is very limited.

timeline.event: Original Cochrane review (Srisurapanont, Jarusuraisin and Kittirattanapaiboon, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2001, Issue 4), whose authors also ran the two amineptine trials.

Cruickshank et al., placebo-controlled trial of mirtazapine for methamphetamine withdrawal in Australian outpatients: no benefit on drop-out, global state or withdrawal symptoms; the only trial in this review judged at low risk of bias for concealment and blinding.
This update: four trials, 125 participants, no medicine shown to reduce withdrawal symptoms.

Acheson et al., meta-analysis of medicines for methamphetamine withdrawal (nine trials of six medicines); by its card in this library it contains the four trials of this review, so the two reviews are not independent evidence.

replication.where_it_stands: The Cochrane review has not been updated since 2009. The later meta-analysis in the library (acheson_2023, card sc_acheson_2023) adds trials of modafinil, amantadine, ibudilast and varenicline and, by that card, also establishes no effective withdrawal medicine. Claims should cite this review for the state of the evidence up to 2008 and for the trial-level risk-of-bias judgments, not for any drug-specific effect size; amineptine, the only medicine with any benefit, was withdrawn from the market in 1999 over misuse.

funding.funder: Internal source: UCLA Integrated Substance Abuse Programs, USA. External sources: none supplied.
funding.affiliations_note: The update was done by UCLA authors (Shoptaw, Kao, Heinzerling, Ling). Srisurapanont, an author of both amineptine trials, developed the protocol and wrote the original 2001 review but is not an author of this update; the update's search, selection, extraction and analysis were done by Shoptaw and Kao.

what_would_settle_it: Adequately powered, registered, placebo-controlled trials of medicines that are actually available (and of non-drug supports for sleep and mood) during the first one to two weeks after stopping amphetamine or methamphetamine, with validated withdrawal and sleep outcomes, systematic recording of adverse effects, follow-up for relapse, and samples that include women and people who are not in treatment.

domains.note: Population (amphetamine withdrawal), interventions (any medicine with or without psychosocial treatment), comparators (placebo or psychosocial treatment alone) and outcomes are specified.
Cochrane protocol published in 2001 before the original review; the change of risk-of-bias method in the update is explained.
Randomized and controlled clinical trials are named as eligible without a stated reason for the choice.

Four databases with strategies in appendices, reference lists, trial registers, conference proceedings and investigators contacted; no language limits; search within 24 months of publication. EMBASE only for the original review.
In the update one author screened titles and abstracts alone; only full-text eligibility was judged by two authors independently.
Data were extracted independently onto forms, with disputes resolved by discussion or the trial's corresponding author.

domains.note: Setting, country, participants, interventions with doses, duration, outcomes and analysis method are given for each trial.

domains.note: Cochrane 2008 domains (sequence generation, concealment, blinding by outcome type, incomplete data, selective reporting) with support for each judgment. The card follows these judgments for the trials, which were not read.

domains.note: Not reported for any trial.

Weighted fixed-effect pooling where heterogeneity was not significant, random effects for the standardized symptom outcome, results also given by medicine, and the medicine named as the source of heterogeneity. Judged met on balance, a close call: the headline drop-out estimate pools two different medicines with opposite results, and the data table pools global state across two different scales as a mean difference although the text says no combined result was calculated.

domains.note: No sensitivity analysis by risk of bias.

domains.note: The discussion and conclusions present the amineptine benefits without weighing the unclear concealment and assessor blinding the review itself recorded for three of the four trials.
Heterogeneity (I2 45% for drop-out, 69% for global state) is attributed to the different medicines and scales, and the global-state results are shown by medicine.
Not investigated or discussed (four trials).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Two critical items are 'no' (13: risk of bias not weighed in the interpretation; 15: publication bias neither investigated nor discussed), which under AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence; critical items 2, 4, 7, 9 and 11 are met. This rates how far the review's pooled numbers can be trusted as unbiased summaries; it is not a judgment of the trials, for which the card follows the review's own Cochrane appraisal and says so (sequence generation low risk in three of four; allocation concealment low risk in one, unclear in three; blinding for subjective outcomes low risk in one, unclear in three; incomplete outcome data and selective reporting judged low risk in all). The review may be cited for the inventory of trials up to May 2008, for its finding that no tested medicine reduced withdrawal symptoms or craving, and for the drop-out and global-state results by medicine, with their imprecision.

key_findings.finding: Searches found 1146 records; 9 full texts were assessed and 4 randomized placebo-controlled trials (125 participants: 37 amineptine, 22 mirtazapine, 66 placebo) were included; 5 studies were excluded with reasons.

Kongsakon 2005 reported significant improvement with mirtazapine as medians, which could not be pooled.

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that no medicine has been shown to relieve amphetamine withdrawal: amineptine had limited benefits (drop-out, global state) but no effect on withdrawal symptoms or craving and was withdrawn from the market in 1999 over misuse; mirtazapine has not been shown to be effective, with few trials.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph; Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice

key_findings.finding: Background (second-hand, not a result of this review): the review cites a survey in which 87.6% of 647 people with amphetamine dependence reported six or more DSM withdrawal signs when the drug was unavailable, and describes withdrawal as starting within a day of last use, with an initial 'crash' that resolves within about a week and milder sleep and appetite changes that generally resolve in about three weeks.
key_findings.locator: Background › Description of the condition, 1st and 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Narrative background citing Schuckit 1999, Gossop 1982 and McGregor 2005; not appraised by the review.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the three global-state trials were too heterogeneous to combine and that no combined result was calculated, but the data table reports a pooled mean difference of -0.27 (-0.54 to -0.01) across the Clinical Global Impression and the BSI Global Severity Index.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › (2) Average score in global state; Data and analyses, Comparison 1, outcome 2
reporting_issues.consequence: A mean difference across two different scales has no common unit; the pooled figure should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The methods say a number needed to treat was calculated for dichotomous outcomes, but no number needed to treat is reported anywhere.
reporting_issues.consequence: No absolute effect is available from the review; drop-out counts per arm appear only in the forest plots (images).

reporting_issues.issue: Adverse events are listed as a primary outcome (patient satisfaction measured by type and number of adverse events), with adherence and deaths as secondary outcomes, but no data on any of them are reported.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Types of outcome measures; Results › Effects of interventions
reporting_issues.consequence: The review cannot be cited for the safety of amineptine or mirtazapine in withdrawal.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and plain-language summary say one trial suggested mirtazapine may reduce hyperarousal and anxiety symptoms; the results section reports only that Kongsakon 2005 found significant improvement on the Amphetamine Withdrawal Questionnaire, in medians that could not be pooled.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Main results; Results › (3) Average score in withdrawal symptoms
reporting_issues.consequence: The symptom-specific benefit attributed to mirtazapine cannot be checked from the review.

reporting_issues.issue: The 'combined' means for the two amineptine trials (age 19.1 years, use history 23.6 months, and time since last use) are unweighted averages of the two trial means (18.5 and 19.6; 23.6 and 23.5; and the two times since last use given in the exposure field), not participant-weighted means.

reporting_issues.consequence: Negligible here; worth knowing if the figures are quoted.

design_detail: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-person crossover trial with counterbalanced order. 46 healthy young adults who had never used psychostimulants took a 20 mg capsule of mixed amphetamine salts (MAS, the Adderall formulation) before each session of one pair of test sessions (one SAT, one cognitive-battery session) and a visually identical placebo capsule before each session of another pair, the pairs about one week apart, after two drug-free baseline sessions. Outcomes: 13 cognitive measures (episodic memory, working memory, inhibitory control, convergent creativity, items from Raven's matrices and the SAT) and a 1–100 rating of how the pill had affected that day's performance; moderation by drug-free baseline ability and by COMT genotype.
can_establish: Whether one 20 mg dose of mixed amphetamine salts, compared with placebo in the same people, changed scores on these 13 laboratory measures in healthy, rested, stimulant-naive young adults, and whether they rated the active capsule as more helpful.
cannot_establish: Effects at other doses, with repeated or long-term use, in people who already use stimulants, after sleep loss or in real study and exam settings; effects smaller than about half a standard deviation on any single measure (the study was sized for d = 0.5); and whether the higher rating of the active capsule reflected a belief about performance or simply noticing a drug, since no blinding check or drug-effect rating was reported.

sample.recruitment: Advertisement: notices around Drexel University and the University of Pennsylvania and e-mail announcements at the University of Pennsylvania, inviting people to tests of memory, creativity, intelligence and personality (p. 498). Participants were paid; the amount is not reported (p. 501).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded: a reported history of conditions contraindicating stimulants (any neurological or psychiatric disease, seizure disorder, high blood pressure, glaucoma, gastrointestinal blockage, heart disease, thyroid problems); use of other stimulants or interacting substances (addictive, psychoactive, neurological and blood-pressure drugs, antihistamines, dietary supplements, weight-loss pills); estimated caffeine intake above 700 mg/day; drug-free blood pressure above 140/90; pregnancy or likely pregnancy; and any previous psychostimulant use, to rule out sensitization and tolerance (p. 498). At each on-pill session a positive urine test (amphetamine, cocaine, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, phencyclidine, cannabis), a positive pregnancy test, or blood pressure above 150/100 shortly before testing led to exclusion (pp. 500–501).
sample.demographics: 46 Caucasian native English speakers, 22 men and 24 women, aged 21–30 (mean 24, SD 2.88) (p. 498). Education, IQ and socioeconomic status are not reported beyond recruitment around two universities.
sample.attrition: No dropouts are reported. Per measure, 36 to 46 participants contributed (Table 2, p. 501): 143 task scores (5.55% of all data) were missing (technical problems 50, failure to understand instructions 9, experimenter error 84), and 22 outlying scores (0.85% of data) led to removal of all that participant's data for the task (p. 501). Missing data are not broken down by condition.
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers answering a call for tests of memory, creativity and intelligence; all stimulant-naive, healthy, Caucasian and low-to-moderate caffeine consumers. The authors note the sample is not representative and that people who have chosen to use stimulants, or who drink a lot of caffeine, might respond differently (p. 504).

exposure.measurement: Experimental administration, double-blind: at each of the four on-pill sessions, one capsule of mixed amphetamine salts or a visually indistinguishable placebo (p. 498; p. 501). The test drug was supplied by the University of Pennsylvania Investigational Drug Service; the paper does not say where the placebo came from (p. 498). Plasma amphetamine was not measured (p. 504).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: a single oral dose of 20 mg mixed amphetamine salts (dextro- and levo-amphetamine in a 3:1 ratio) before each of the two sessions of the MAS condition (one SAT session, one cognitive-battery session, at least 2 days apart); the MAS and placebo pairs were about 1 week apart (p. 498; Fig. 2, p. 501). Testing began about 75 minutes after the capsule (p. 501). One dose only; dose was not varied (p. 504).
exposure.polysubstance: Other stimulants and interacting drugs were excluded and checked by urine tests at each on-pill session (pp. 498, 500–501). Caffeine above about 700 mg/day was excluded; caffeine and sleep in the previous 24 hours were recorded at each on-pill session, but caffeine intake is not reported in the results. Alcohol and tobacco use are not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: No previous psychostimulant use by self-report (p. 498); urine drug tests at every on-pill session (pp. 500–501).

comparison.controls: The same participants under placebo (within-person crossover). Two drug-free baseline sessions, always first, were used only to define baseline ability for the moderation analyses (pp. 500–501).
comparison.matching: Within-person comparison; drug order and test-version order were counterbalanced and entered as between-person factors in every analysis (pp. 500–501).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the drug–placebo contrast, since each person is their own control. For moderation, baseline ability came from separate drug-free sessions rather than from placebo scores, which avoids regression to the mean (p. 497).

outcomes.instruments: 13 measures (pp. 498–500): face recognition, word recall and word recognition after about 2 hours of other testing (episodic memory); Digit Span forward and backward and Object-2-Back omissions (working memory); Go/No-go commission errors and Flanker inhibition cost (inhibitory control); Remote Associates Test and Group Embedded Figures (convergent creativity); 12 items of Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices; SAT-style Verbal (48 items) and Math (27 items) sections. Perceived drug effect: a 1–100 line rating of how the pill affected performance on that day's tests (1 = impaired extremely, 50 = no effect, 100 = improved extremely), asked after the cognitive battery only, not after the SAT sessions (pp. 500–501, 503). Three versions of each task. COMT val158met genotype (genotyping method not described).
outcomes.validity_norms: Several tasks were assembled from items of standardized tests (Raven's, SAT practice books); versions were pilot-tested for comparable difficulty (p. 498). No norms or reliability data are reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Enhancement = better score on MAS than on placebo in a 2 (drug) × 2 (drug order) × 2 (version order) mixed ANOVA; moderation = drug × baseline-group or drug × COMT interaction. The stated aim was to detect at least moderate enhancement, Cohen's d of 0.5 or more (abstract, p. 496).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: results are reported without correction for multiple comparisons, which the authors call a lenient approach (p. 501). A MANOVA across the 13 measures served as the omnibus test.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind administration (p. 501); outcomes are objective test scores. Blinding integrity was not assessed.

analysis.effect_sizes: The paper reports F and p values only. Drug main effects were all non-significant (Table 1, p. 499); the smallest p was for Remote Associations, F(1, 42) = 2.56, p = .12. MANOVA across the 13 measures F(13, 13) = 1.71, p = .17 (p. 501). Editors' calculation from Table 2 (MAS minus placebo divided by the mean of the two SDs, signed so that positive means better on MAS): face recognition +0.10, word recall +0.02, word recognition −0.10, Digit Span backward +0.04, forward −0.04, Object-2-Back +0.03, Go/No-go +0.10, Flanker 0.00, Remote Associates +0.25, Embedded Figures +0.08, Raven −0.04, SAT Math −0.11, SAT Verbal −0.06. Editors' within-person d from each drug F and n (sign from Table 2): −0.16 to +0.24, with approximate upper 95% limits from 0.13 to 0.53 (highest for Remote Associates). Perceived enhancement 55.18 (SD 14.87) on MAS vs 50.25 (SD 3.95) on placebo, F(1, 40) = 4.09, p = .05 (p. 503); editors' within-person d about 0.30 (95% CI about 0.00 to 0.61).
analysis.covariates: None beyond the design factors (drug order, version order). Sleep before MAS and placebo sessions was compared separately (p. 502).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No trial registration or protocol is mentioned. The 13 measures and the moderation hypotheses are described as a priori (pp. 498, 502).
analysis.selective_reporting: All 13 measures are reported with means and SDs (Table 2) and full ANOVA results (Table 1). Not reported: the personality, mood and attributional-style questionnaires given in the SAT sessions (set aside as not relevant; p. 501), blood pressure before and after testing, caffeine intake, and any question on which capsule participants thought they had. Further moderation results are in Supplementary Table 1 (an online supplement, not among the files read), described as extraneous to the predictions (pp. 502–503).
analysis.power: The sample of 46 was chosen to give 95% power to detect d = 0.5 on any single measure (p. 498). Editors' calculation: a two-sided paired test at alpha .05 with n = 46 has about 91% power for a within-person d of 0.5 (95% corresponds to a one-sided test), falling to about 83% with the 36 participants who had Embedded Figures data; the MANOVA's degrees of freedom imply about 29 complete cases (reporting issues). Effects around d = 0.2 on single measures could not be detected or excluded.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A single 20 mg dose of mixed amphetamine salts changed none of 13 laboratory measures of memory, working memory, inhibitory control, creativity, matrix reasoning or SAT-type items relative to placebo in 46 stimulant-naive, rested young adults; the largest observed difference was about a quarter of a standard deviation (Remote Associates, not significant). Participants rated the active capsule slightly more helpful (55 vs 50 on a scale where 50 meant no effect, p = .05), and the size of each person's rating difference did not track their actual change in scores. Moderation by baseline ability or COMT genotype appeared in a minority of uncorrected subgroup tests.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls the trial adequately powered and concludes that MAS has no more than small effects on cognition in healthy young adults (p. 496), which fits the data for the average participant at this dose. Three statements go further than the results. (1) The abstract says MAS enhanced lower-ability participants on word recall, embedded figures and Raven's matrices; these come from uncorrected tests in subgroups of roughly 16 to 20 people, and the drug × baseline interaction for Raven's was itself not significant (p = .10; p. 502). (2) The discussion calls the effect on judgments of enhancement “small but reliable” (p. 504), although it rests on one uncorrected test at p = .05. (3) The abstract and discussion frame the ratings as an illusory perception of enhancement (pp. 496, 504), but with no blinding check or drug-effect rating, participants may simply have noticed the active drug and assumed it helped. A headline such as “Adderall does not make you smarter” would overstate the paper: it tested one dose, once, in drug-naive volunteers on laboratory tasks, and its intervals leave room for small to moderate effects on single measures.

timeline.event: Farah et al. (Psychopharmacology), an earlier study by the same group of mixed amphetamine salts and creativity; the present paper reports replicating its finding that lower baseline performers gained more on Embedded Figures (p. 502).
Smith and Farah review of more than fifty experiments on amphetamine and methylphenidate in healthy young adults: a roughly even mix of significant enhancement and null findings (p. 497).
Ilieva, Hook and Farah meta-analysis includes this trial (Hedges' g 0.05 inhibitory control, 0.01 working memory, 0.01 delayed episodic memory) and uses its data to impute within-person correlations.

replication.where_it_stands: No direct replication was read. The same group's 2015 meta-analysis of 48 double-blind placebo-controlled studies puts the average single-dose effect of amphetamine or methylphenidate in healthy adults at about 0.1 to 0.2 standard deviations for inhibitory control and working memory, which is consistent with a null result for any one dose and measure in a sample of this size.

funding.funder: Office of Naval Research, grant N000140710034 (p. 504). Study drug supplied by the University of Pennsylvania Investigational Drug Service (p. 498).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: All three authors at the University of Pennsylvania; the senior author (Farah) co-wrote the 2011 review that motivated the design and is senior author of the related 2015 meta-analysis. Published in a special issue on cognitive enhancers (p. 496). Military research funding is recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered, multi-site crossover trial large enough to detect d = 0.2 on single measures, testing more than one dose, including people who already use stimulants for study and people after sleep restriction, with real academic outcomes, a blinding check, drug-effect ratings and plasma amphetamine levels.

domains.note: Participants were randomly assigned to capsule order with counterbalancing (24 vs 22), but sequence generation and allocation concealment are not described (pp. 500–501).

domains.domain: Bias arising from period and carryover effects (crossover)
domains.note: About one week separated the MAS and placebo pairs of sessions; drug order was counterbalanced and entered in every analysis, and no drug × drug-order interaction was significant (MANOVA p = .83; Table 1).

Identical capsules and double-blind administration, but blinding was not checked, and an active stimulant may be recognizable. Analyses used available data per measure rather than every randomized participant.

5.55% of scores missing plus 0.85% removed as outliers, taking the whole task's data for that person; 36 to 46 of 46 participants per measure. Reasons were mostly technical or experimenter error, but the split by condition is not reported.
Objective test scores under double-blind conditions. The perceived-enhancement rating is self-reported by participants who may have recognized the active drug: some concerns for that outcome only.

No registration. All 13 a priori measures are reported, but there is no multiplicity correction, moderation was tested several ways, mood questionnaires and blood pressure were collected and not reported, and a supplementary table of results is not discussed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The null drug effects are credible within the design: within-person comparison, identical capsules, counterbalanced order and all prespecified measures reported with means and SDs. Concerns are the undescribed randomization, missing data of up to 22% on two measures, an unverified blind (which matters most for the perceived-enhancement rating) and uncorrected moderation tests. Cite for: no detectable effect of one 20 mg dose on these 13 measures in stimulant-naive young adults, and a small difference in rated benefit that did not track actual performance. Do not cite for: effects in people who use stimulants, at other doses or with repeated use, or for enhancement in low-ability or genotype subgroups.

key_findings.finding: Participants were 46 Caucasian native English speakers (22 men, 24 women) aged 21–30 (mean 24, SD 2.88), recruited by advertisement around Drexel University and the University of Pennsylvania; people were excluded if they reported a history of conditions that rule out stimulants or had ever used psychostimulants. As study conditions, each took a 20 mg capsule of mixed amphetamine salts before each of two test sessions (one SAT session, one cognitive-battery session) and a visually identical placebo capsule before two other sessions, double-blind, with order counterbalanced (24 had the drug first).
key_findings.locator: 2.1 Participants; 2.2 Drug (p. 498); 2.4 Procedure, 1st paragraph (p. 500); 2.4.3, continued, and Fig. 2 (p. 501)

key_findings.finding: Across all 13 measures together, performance on the drug did not differ from placebo (MANOVA F(13, 13) = 1.71, p = .17), and the drug's effect did not depend on whether it came first or second (F(13, 13) = .59, p = .83) or on test-version order (F(13, 13) = 1.28, p = .33).
key_findings.locator: 3.1 Effects of mixed amphetamine salts, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Tested one by one, none of the 13 measures improved on the drug: no drug main effect was significant, the smallest p being .12 (Remote Associations, F(1, 42) = 2.56). Placebo and drug means were, for example, 27.61 and 28.05 faces recognized, 4.50 and 4.59 words recalled, 8.19 and 8.11 Raven items, 13.76 and 13.07 SAT Math items, and 30.73 and 30.29 SAT Verbal items. Editors' calculation from Table 2: standardized drug-minus-placebo differences ranged from −0.11 to +0.25, the largest for Remote Associates.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 499); Table 2 (p. 501); 3.1, 2nd paragraph (p. 502)

key_findings.finding: The sample was sized for 95% power to detect a medium effect (Cohen's d = .5) on any single measure, so smaller effects could not be ruled out. Editors' calculation from each drug F and n: within-person effect sizes from −0.16 to +0.24, with approximate upper 95% limits of 0.13 to 0.53.
key_findings.locator: 1.2.4 Statistical power
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation of power: about 91% for a two-sided paired test with 46 people; the stated 95% corresponds to a one-sided test.

key_findings.finding: A three-way drug × drug order × version order interaction was significant, without correction, on 5 of the 13 measures (Face Recognition F(1, 40) = 16.01; Flanker F(1, 39) = 4.76; Remote Associations F(1, 42) = 8.44; Embedded Figures F(1, 32) = 10.68; SAT Math F(1, 41) = 4.56); the authors found no obvious interpretation.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 499); 3.1, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 502)

key_findings.finding: Self-reported sleep before drug and placebo sessions did not differ (t(41) = .91, p = .37 for the cognitive sessions; t(45) = .74, p = .47 for the SAT sessions); if anything participants slept slightly more before drug sessions (7.12 vs 6.89 hours before the cognitive sessions).
key_findings.locator: 3.1, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Baseline ability, measured in separate drug-free sessions, moderated the drug effect on Word Recall (F(1, 36) = 4.78, p = .04) and Embedded Figures (F(1, 28) = 8.48, p < .01), with a non-significant trend for Raven's matrices (F(1, 29) = 2.83, p = .10) and none on the other measures. In below-median performers alone the drug improved Word Recall (F(1, 16) = 6.71), Embedded Figures (F(1, 12) = 8.41) and Raven (F(1, 16) = 5.36), while above-median performers tended to score lower on the drug (Fig. 3). All tests were uncorrected.
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Moderation of MAS effect by baseline performance, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Fig. 3

key_findings.finding: COMT genotype results were sparse and inconsistent: in regression the genotype effect on the drug-minus-placebo difference was significant only for SAT Math (b = .35, t = 2.38, p = .02); comparing the two homozygous groups, the multivariate test was not significant (F(5, 1) = .64, p = .73) and the only univariate interaction was SAT Math (F(1, 11) = 13.06), where the drug's main effect in this subsample lowered scores (F(1, 11) = 5.63, p = .04); in val/val participants alone the drug improved no measure (all p > .24). Genotype counts and the genotyping method are not reported.
key_findings.locator: 3.3 Moderation of MAS effect by COMT genotype, 1st–4th paragraphs; Fig. 4

key_findings.finding: The twist: participants rated the active capsule as slightly more helpful than placebo, 55.18 (SD 14.87) vs 50.25 (SD 3.95) on a 1–100 line on which 50 meant no effect and 75 meant somewhat improved (F(1, 40) = 4.09, p = .05). The rating concerned that day's tests and was asked only after the cognitive battery. Editors' calculation: a difference of about 5 points, within-person d about 0.30 (95% CI about 0.00 to 0.61).
key_findings.locator: 2.3.6 Perceived drug effect (p. 500); 3.4 Perceived enhancement, 1st paragraph (p. 503)

key_findings.finding: Feeling helped did not go with being helped: the difference in rated benefit (drug minus placebo) was not significantly correlated with the difference in performance on 10 of the 11 measures rated, correlated only with Go/No-go (r = .33, p = .04), and did not correlate significantly with a composite of all measures (r = −.06, p = .76).
key_findings.locator: 3.4 Perceived enhancement, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The minus sign of the composite correlation is visible on the rendered page but missing from the PDF's text layer.

key_findings.finding: 143 task scores (5.55% of all data) were missing (technical problems 50, failure to understand instructions 9, experimenter error 84), and 22 outlying scores (0.85% of data) led to dropping that participant's data for the task, so per-measure samples were 36 to 46.
key_findings.locator: 2.5.1 Outlier removal; 2.5.2 Missing data; Table 2

key_findings.finding: All results are reported without correction for multiple comparisons, an approach the authors describe as lenient and as raising the risk of false positives.
key_findings.locator: 2.5.3 Statistical tests

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that a standard clinical dose of a drug commonly used for enhancement did not enhance cognition in an adequately powered study, so any effects in healthy, rested young adults are likely small. Their limitations: a single dose, no plasma drug levels, and a sample restricted to stimulant-naive, low-to-moderate caffeine consumers.
key_findings.locator: 4.1, 1st paragraph (begins on p. 503, conclusion on p. 504); 4.2 Limitations of the present study (p. 504)

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints the Object-2-Back drug main effect as F(1, 41) = 1.13 with p = .74, the same p as that row's three-way interaction (F = .11). With placebo and drug means of 8.98 and 8.84 omissions (Table 2) a very small F is expected, so the F value is the likelier misprint (editors' calculation: F(1, 41) = 1.13 would give p of about .29).
reporting_issues.consequence: The null result stands either way, but this F value should not be used to compute an effect size.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 2.4 says 24 participants received the drug in Sessions 3 and 4 and 22 in Sessions 6 and 7, but Session 3 was a drug-free baseline session and the on-pill sessions were 4 to 7 (Fig. 2; 2.4.2).
reporting_issues.consequence: Read as 24 drug-first participants (Sessions 4 and 5) and 22 placebo-first; the order groups are otherwise as described.

reporting_issues.issue: The MANOVA across the 13 measures is reported as F(13, 13) = 1.71. With a within-person drug factor and four between-person order cells, an error df of 13 implies that only about 29 participants with complete data on all 13 measures entered the test, not 46 (editors' calculation: N − 4 − 13 + 1 = 13); the paper does not say so.
reporting_issues.consequence: The primary multivariate test had much less power than the sample size suggests; the univariate tests on 36 to 46 people carry more of the evidence.

reporting_issues.issue: The COMT multivariate tests are reported as F(5, 1) = .64 and F(2, 1) = .27: numerator degrees of freedom of 5 and 2 do not match the 13 measures said to be analysed, and an error df of 1 leaves essentially no power. The regressions on val load report F(3, 43) (editors' calculation: this implies 47 participants, whereas 46 were enrolled and 45 had SAT data), and one interaction is printed as p < .00. Genotype counts and the genotyping method are not given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The genotype analyses cannot be checked from the paper, and the multivariate COMT tests are uninformative; the SAT Math interaction rests on single uncorrected tests in a small homozygous subsample.

reporting_issues.issue: Go/No-go was scored as commission errors (fewer is better), but the paper does not say how the drug-minus-placebo difference was signed when it reports the one significant correlation between perceived and actual enhancement (r = .33, p = .04).
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of that correlation cannot be confirmed; with 11 uncorrected correlations, one result near p = .05 is about what chance alone would produce.

reporting_issues.issue: The caption of Fig. 3 describes groups split by overall baseline performance, while the text says the median split was made separately for each measure, so that different participants fall in the upper and lower groups for different measures.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the text describes the analysis actually run.

reporting_issues.issue: Personality, mood and attributional-style questionnaires were given in the SAT sessions, and blood pressure and caffeine intake were recorded at each on-pill session, but none of these results is reported, and participants were not asked which capsule they thought they had taken.
reporting_issues.consequence: There is no manipulation check showing whether participants felt the drug, which is central to reading the higher rating of the active capsule as an illusion of enhancement.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints the Raven drug × drug-order interaction as F(1, 33) = .05 with p = .80. An F of .05 on 1 and 33 degrees of freedom gives p of about .82 to .83 (editors' calculation), the value printed for the same F in that measure's three-way interaction row (F = .05, p = .83).
reporting_issues.consequence: A misprint of the p value or of the F; the interaction is null either way and no conclusion changes.

design_detail: Systematic search with random-effects meta-analyses of double-blind, placebo-controlled studies of a single oral dose of amphetamine or methylphenidate in healthy young and middle-aged adults, on four constructs: inhibitory control, working memory, short-term episodic memory (tested within 30 minutes of learning) and delayed episodic memory (1 hour to 1 week). 48 articles (44 published reports, 3 unpublished data sets, 1 dissertation; 1,409 participants). Primary effect size: Hedges' g scaled by the placebo-condition SD; secondary: g scaled by the SD of within-person change. Publication bias assessed with funnel plots, trim-and-fill and fail-safe N.
can_establish: The average size of the effect of one oral dose of amphetamine or methylphenidate, compared with placebo, on laboratory tests of these four functions in healthy adults, in studies published or obtained up to December 2012, and how sensitive those averages are to apparent publication bias.
cannot_establish: Effects of repeated or long-term use, of use for real studying, exams or work, after sleep loss, in people with ADHD, children or older adults; effects on attention, motivation or energy (not analysed); whether amphetamine and methylphenidate truly differ (moderator tests rest on few studies); or how biased the included trials were, since no risk-of-bias assessment was made.

sample.recruitment: PubMed and PsycInfo searched with amphetamine or methylphenidate combined with listed task and construct terms; reference lists of four reviews; the list of articles under review by an American Academy of Neurology committee on cognitive enhancement on which the last author serves; research published to the end of December 2012. Twenty researchers were asked for unpublished data and 14 requests were made for missing data from studies of the past 10 years, yielding two data sets in progress, extra effect-size data from four published reports and an unpublished pilot data set from the authors' laboratory (p. 1070).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: any report format (journal articles, dissertations, conference presentations, unpublished data); English only; young and middle-aged adults; double-blind placebo-controlled design; a single oral dose given before testing; outcomes in the four constructs, with measures chosen by an a priori hierarchy (Table 1, pp. 1072–1073). Excluded: children, older adults, criminal or mentally ill samples, sleep deprivation, intravenous dosing, testing under TMS, dosing after learning, repeated dosing (pp. 1070–1071).
sample.demographics: Per-study N, recruitment target, age, percentage of men, years of education, psychiatric screening, caffeine restriction, drug and dose are in Tables 2–5 (pp. 1078–1083). Study sizes range from 8 to 207 (Table 2). Most studies are within-person designs. Several tabulated sample sizes are inconsistent across tables (reporting issues).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. 19 otherwise eligible studies could not be used because effect-size data were unavailable, and missing effects were not imputed (pp. 1071, 1074).
sample.selection_effects: Two databases, English only (7 non-English studies excluded), four full texts not retrievable and 19 eligible studies without usable data; the search ended in December 2012 and the paper appeared in 2015. Psychiatric screening ranged from structured interviews to self-report or was not described. The delayed-memory evidence is dominated by one laboratory's low-dose, all-male studies (p. 1085).

exposure.measurement: As administered in each trial: oral amphetamine (including mixed amphetamine salts) or methylphenidate, a single dose, double-blind against placebo.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as tabulated: amphetamine 5 to 30 mg and methylphenidate 10 to 40 mg (Tables 2–5), coded high at or above 20 mg amphetamine or 40 mg methylphenidate and low otherwise (p. 1073); where a study tested several doses, effects were averaged (p. 1075). Testing began 30 minutes to 4.5 hours after amphetamine and 40 minutes to 4.5 hours after methylphenidate (p. 1070).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed beyond eligibility. Instruction to avoid caffeine on the test day was coded as a moderator and was not significant for any construct.

comparison.controls: Placebo, double-blind, in the same people (most studies) or in a separate group (between-person studies).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Baseline cognitive ability and dopamine-related genotypes (COMT, DRD2), which may moderate stimulant effects, could not be examined for lack of data (p. 1085).

outcomes.instruments: Inhibitory control: stop-signal, go/no-go, Wisconsin Card Sorting, ID/ED, Flanker, Stroop, antisaccade. Working memory: n-back (2- and 3-back only), rapid information processing, Sternberg, Digit Span, CANTAB spatial working memory, spatial delayed response. Episodic memory: free and cued recall and recognition tests, split by retention interval (Table 1, pp. 1072–1073).
outcomes.validity_norms: Measures chosen by an a priori hierarchy favouring error over reaction-time measures unless accuracy was at ceiling (p. 1071). Suspected floor or ceiling effects were coded and tested as a moderator.
outcomes.operationalization: Enhancement = positive Hedges' g for drug minus placebo, scaled by the placebo-condition SD (primary) or by the SD of within-person change (secondary); one averaged effect per study per construct (pp. 1074–1075).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Eight pooled estimates (four constructs, two metrics) plus moderator tests for up to seven moderators per construct.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Eligibility decided independently by two authors with consensus; coding by the first author, with a random 44% of means and SDs coded independently by the second author (pp. 1071, 1074).

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects Hedges' g with 95% CI (pp. 1077, 1084–1085). Inhibitory control: 0.20 (0.11 to 0.30), 24 studies, Q(23) = 7.82, I2 = 0; change metric 0.19 (0.11 to 0.26). Working memory: 0.13 (−0.02 to 0.27), 20 studies, Q(19) = 7.74, I2 = 0; change metric 0.13 (0.06 to 0.20), 23 studies; trim-and-fill 0.06 (−0.08 to 0.20). Short-term episodic memory: 0.20 (0.01 to 0.38), 12 studies, Q(11) = 4.44, I2 = 0; change metric 0.22 (0.09 to 0.35); trim-and-fill 0.12 (−0.06 to 0.29); fail-safe N 2. Delayed episodic memory: 0.45 (0.27 to 0.63), 11 studies, Q(10) = 9.67, I2 = 0; change metric 0.44 (0.26 to 0.62); trim-and-fill 0.26 (0.04 to 0.47); fail-safe N 59. No tau-squared or prediction intervals; per-study confidence intervals and forest plots are not shown. Trim-and-fill values are d without Hedges' correction, from published studies only (p. 1076).
analysis.covariates: Moderators: drug (amphetamine vs methylphenidate), dose (high vs low), caffeine restriction, percentage of men (meta-regression), suspected floor or ceiling effects, other reasons to publish a null result, and for working memory, stimulus type and subprocess (pp. 1071–1075).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; an a priori outcome-selection procedure is described (Table 1).
analysis.selective_reporting: Moderator and publication-bias results for the secondary (change-score) analyses are not detailed, being described as qualitatively similar (p. 1076).
analysis.power: Not addressed. With 11 to 24 mostly small studies per pool, I2 of 0 everywhere gives little information about true heterogeneity, and moderator tests rest on few studies per level.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across double-blind placebo-controlled studies of one oral dose in healthy adults, average effects were small: about 0.2 SD for inhibitory control (unchanged by trim-and-fill), 0.13 SD for working memory (not significant in the primary metric; 0.06 after trim-and-fill), 0.20 SD for short-term episodic memory (0.12 and not significant after trim-and-fill; fail-safe N of 2) and 0.45 SD for delayed episodic memory (0.26 after trim-and-fill), the last concentrated in one laboratory's low-dose, all-male studies with long retention intervals.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports small but significant effects on inhibitory control and short-term episodic memory and a medium effect on delayed memory, says the working-memory and long-term-memory effects were qualified by evidence of publication bias, and concludes that the effects are probably modest overall (p. 1069). It omits that the short-term memory estimate also lost significance after trim-and-fill and could be nullified by two null studies (p. 1084). The discussion says the results “confirm the reality of cognitive enhancing effects for normal healthy adults” (p. 1086), firmer than evidence that was not appraised for risk of bias and that is sensitive to publication-bias adjustment for three of four constructs, and it suggests that small effects could decide an entrance or licensing examination, which was not studied (p. 1086). A headline that study drugs make healthy people smarter would overstate this paper, and so would one saying they do nothing: the defensible summary is a small average lift on laboratory tests after one dose, clearest for inhibitory control.

timeline.event: Repantis et al. systematic review of modafinil and methylphenidate: not able to show positive effects in healthy people on objective tests (as cited, p. 1069).
Smith and Farah review: large, small and null effects all reported, leaving the size and robustness of effects uncertain; this meta-analysis was designed to quantify them (pp. 1069–1070).
Ilieva, Boland and Farah crossover trial, included here (Hedges' g 0.05 inhibitory control, 0.01 working memory, 0.01 delayed memory) and used to impute within-person correlations.

replication.where_it_stands: As read here, the pooled estimate for single-dose effects in healthy adults up to 2012. Its delayed-memory estimate depends on a cluster of studies from one laboratory and on publication-bias adjustment. Later meta-analyses on the project's methylphenidate list (Roberts et al., 2020) were not read for this card.

funding.funder: Not reported. The acknowledgments thank colleagues for feedback and Angela Duckworth for access to the Comprehensive Meta-Analysis software (p. 1086).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: All authors at the University of Pennsylvania. The review includes the authors' own crossover trial (Ilieva et al., 2013) and unpublished data from the last author's laboratory (Farah, 2012), uses the 2013 trial's data to impute within-person correlations (Note 1, p. 1086), and drew candidate studies from an American Academy of Neurology committee list on which the last author serves (p. 1070). Recorded as a flag for closer reading.

what_would_settle_it: An updated, registered meta-analysis with risk-of-bias assessment and individual participant data, together with preregistered multi-laboratory trials of delayed episodic memory in both sexes at several doses, would show whether the memory effects hold outside the single laboratory that produced the largest estimates.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Healthy young and middle-aged adults; one oral dose of amphetamine or methylphenidate; double-blind placebo; four cognitive constructs with an a priori outcome hierarchy (pp. 1070–1073).
No protocol or registration mentioned.

A double-blind placebo-controlled design was required, a criterion that aimed to maximize methodological quality (p. 1070); within- and between-person designs were combined with a stated rationale (p. 1074).

Two databases with keywords listed, four reviews' reference lists, an expert committee's list, 20 researchers contacted and grey literature eligible; but English only (7 reports excluded) without justification, no trial-registry search, and the search ended in December 2012, more than two years before publication. Judged as written under the project's reading of item 4 (decision p-amstar2-item4).
Eligibility determined independently by the first and second authors, disagreements resolved by consensus (p. 1071).

The first author coded all studies; the second independently coded a random 44% of means and SDs, with intraclass correlation above .99 (p. 1074), which meets the item's sample-with-good-agreement criterion. Moderator coding was not double-checked.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Only counts by reason (Figure 1, p. 1073); no list of excluded studies.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Tables 2–5 give N, recruitment, age, sex, education, psychiatric screening, caffeine restriction, drug, dose, test and design; the drug-to-test interval and country are not given per study, and several sample sizes are misprinted.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No risk-of-bias tool. Quality was handled only through the double-blind placebo-controlled eligibility criterion; randomization of order, allocation concealment and selective reporting were not assessed.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Random-effects model with a stated rationale; Hedges' g; one averaged effect per study and construct; within-person correlations imputed with a sensitivity analysis (largest change 0.02). For within-person designs the primary standard error uses the two-independent-groups formula (p. 1075), which widens their intervals and is conservative.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Risk of bias was not assessed, so its impact was not analysed.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The interpretation addresses publication bias and confounded moderators, but not the risk of bias of individual studies, which was not assessed.

Q and I2 reported for every pool (all I2 = 0); moderator analyses were run regardless of heterogeneity, and the confounding of dose, sex and laboratory in the delayed-memory pool is discussed (p. 1085).

Funnel plots, trim-and-fill and fail-safe N on published studies, with their consequences discussed for each construct; the fail-safe N is read inconsistently with the paper's own threshold (reporting issues).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No funding or competing-interest statement, although the authors' own trial and unpublished data are included.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Five critical items are not met (2: no protocol; 4: English-only search without justification and no registry search; 7: no list of excluded studies; 9 and 13: no risk-of-bias assessment), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2. This rates how far the pooled numbers can be trusted as unbiased summaries, not the paper's value: the review restricted itself to double-blind placebo-controlled studies, sought unpublished data, tabulated every study and tested publication bias for each construct. Cite for: small average effects of one dose on inhibitory control (about 0.2 SD), and the sensitivity of the working-memory and episodic-memory estimates to publication-bias adjustment. Do not cite the delayed-memory estimate of 0.45 without its trim-and-fill value of 0.26 and its dependence on one laboratory.

key_findings.finding: The review searched PubMed and PsycInfo, four reviews' reference lists and an American Academy of Neurology committee's list for research published to the end of December 2012, and asked 20 researchers for unpublished data. Only English-language reports were eligible; a double-blind placebo-controlled design and a single oral dose before testing were required; studies of children, older adults, criminal or mentally ill samples and sleep deprivation were excluded.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Search Strategies; Criteria for Study Eligibility

key_findings.finding: Of 1,799 records (1,505 after removing duplicates), 1,304 were excluded on title and 201 were assessed; exclusions included 73 for an out-of-scope cognitive construct, 18 for lacking a double-blind placebo-controlled design, 7 for language and 19 for unavailable effect-size data. 48 articles were analysed (44 published reports, 3 unpublished data sets, 1 dissertation), with 1,409 participants.
key_findings.locator: Process of Determining Study Eligibility (p. 1071); Figure 1 (p. 1073)
key_findings.note: The text gives the 18 design exclusions in words (Eighteen reports, p. 1071); the numeral appears in Figure 1, an image without a text layer, checked on the rendered page.

key_findings.finding: Inhibitory control (24 studies): a small, consistent improvement of about a fifth of a standard deviation, Hedges' g = 0.20 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.30), and 0.19 (0.11 to 0.26) in the change-score metric; no heterogeneity (Q(23) = 7.82, p > .99, I2 = 0.00); no moderator significant (all ps > .20). The funnel plot of the 22 published studies was roughly symmetrical, trim-and-fill removed no study, and the fail-safe N was 39.
key_findings.locator: Results › Stimulants' Effects on Healthy Inhibitory Control, 1st–3rd paragraphs; Table 2 (pp. 1078–1079); Figure 2 (p. 1084)

key_findings.finding: Working memory: g = 0.13 (−0.02 to 0.27) from 20 studies, not significant; 0.13 (0.06 to 0.20) from 23 studies in the change-score metric; Q(19) = 7.74, p = .99, I2 = 0.00; no moderators. In published studies only, the funnel plot was slightly negatively skewed, and trim-and-fill (4 data points trimmed) gave a non-significant d = 0.06 (−0.08 to 0.20), and d = 0.06 (−0.03 to 0.15) in the change-score metric.
key_findings.locator: Results › Stimulants' Effects on Healthy Working Memory, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Table 3 (pp. 1080–1081); Figure 3 (p. 1084)

key_findings.finding: Short-term episodic memory (tested within 30 minutes): of fourteen effect sizes, two outliers were removed (SAMD −8.53 and 2.18); from 12 studies g = 0.20 (0.01 to 0.38), and 0.22 (0.09 to 0.35) in the change-score metric; Q(11) = 4.44, p = .96, I2 = 0.00; no moderators (all ps > .64). In the 11 published studies, trim-and-fill (3 trimmed) gave a non-significant d = 0.12 (−0.06 to 0.29), and the fail-safe N was 2, which the authors say casts doubt on the effect's robustness.
key_findings.locator: Results › Short-term Episodic Memory, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 1077) and 3rd paragraph (p. 1084); Table 4 (p. 1082); Figure 4 (p. 1084)

key_findings.finding: Delayed episodic memory (1 hour to 1 week): one outlier removed (SAMD 3.35); from 11 studies g = 0.45 (0.27 to 0.63), a medium effect, and 0.44 (0.26 to 0.62) in the change-score metric; I2 = 0.00, Q(10) = 9.67, p = .47. The funnel plot was negatively skewed; trim-and-fill (5 trimmed) gave d = 0.26 (0.04 to 0.47); the fail-safe N was 59.
key_findings.locator: Results › Delayed Episodic Memory, 1st–3rd paragraphs; Table 5 (p. 1083); Figure 5 (p. 1084)

key_findings.finding: Who drives the delayed-memory effect: effects were larger in samples with more men (Q(1) = 7.44, p < .01, β = 0.01) and at low doses (g = 0.64, 0.40 to 0.88) than at high doses (0.20, −0.08 to 0.48; Q(1) = 5.49, p = .02). But every low-dose study came from one research group, tested only men and tended to use longer retention intervals (up to 1 week), and the six largest effects came from that laboratory; among high-dose tests the share of men was 48% to 70% and retention, with one exception, 2 hours. No other moderator was significant (all ps > .52).
key_findings.locator: Results › Delayed Episodic Memory, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Discussion › Summary and Interpretation of Results, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The 48% is the text's figure (p. 1084); Table 5 lists 50%, 61.11% and 70% for three high-dose studies and does not report the fourth (p. 1083; reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Amphetamine and methylphenidate were not shown to differ: drug type, dose, caffeine restriction, sex ratio, suspected floor or ceiling effects and other reasons to publish did not significantly moderate the effects on inhibitory control (all ps > .20), working memory (no p values given; stimulus type and working-memory subprocess were also tested) or short-term episodic memory (all ps > .64). In the delayed-memory pool only sex ratio and dose were significant moderators (all other ps > .52).
key_findings.locator: Results › Inhibitory Control, 2nd paragraph; Working Memory, 2nd paragraph; Short-term Episodic Memory, 2nd paragraph (p. 1077); Delayed Episodic Memory, 2nd paragraph (p. 1084)

key_findings.finding: The primary effect size scales the drug-minus-placebo difference by the placebo-condition SD, so that within- and between-person designs share one metric. Within-person correlations, unreported in the primary studies, were imputed from three data sets, one of them the authors' own 2013 trial; repeating the main analyses with uniform correlations of .2, .5 and .8 changed effect sizes by at most g = 0.02.
key_findings.locator: Statistical Methods › Effect Size Metrics (pp. 1074–1075); Notes 1 and 2 (p. 1086)

key_findings.finding: Eligibility was decided independently by the first two authors with disagreements resolved by consensus; all studies were coded by the first author, and the second independently coded a random 44% of the means and SDs, with intraclass correlation above .99. No risk-of-bias tool was applied; study quality was handled only by requiring a double-blind placebo-controlled design.
key_findings.locator: Research Design: Methodological Quality (p. 1070); Process of Determining Study Eligibility (p. 1071); Coding Procedures, last paragraph (p. 1074)

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude in the abstract that the effect on the examined facets of healthy cognition is probably modest overall, that a small advantage may sometimes be valuable, and that it is possible that healthy people use stimulants to enhance energy and motivation more than cognition. The discussion says the results cannot address individual differences or motivational effects but confirm the reality of cognitive-enhancing effects for healthy adults in general while showing them to be modest in size, and that the findings should temper more sceptical assessments.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 1069); Discussion › Neuroethical Implications, 2nd and 3rd (last two) paragraphs (p. 1086)

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 5 (delayed episodic memory) the sample sizes disagree with those given for the same studies elsewhere: Ilieva et al. (2013) is listed with N = 18, against 43 in Tables 2 and 3 and 46 participants in Note 1; Mintzer and Griffiths (2003) with 16 (20 in Table 3) and (2007) with 20 (18 in Table 3 and Note 1). For the seven studies in both Tables 4 and 5, each N in Table 5 equals the N that Table 4 gives the preceding study (Table 4: 18, 14, 12, 12, 24, 16, 36; Table 5: 44, 18, 14, 12, 12, 24, 16), which points to a one-row offset in the printed column (editors' observation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 5 cannot be used to check study weights in the delayed-memory pool. Figure 5 suggests the analysis used the correct sizes: its most precise point (standard error about 0.21) lies at an effect near 0, as expected for Ilieva et al. (2013) with about 44 participants rather than 18, and the point at about 0.8 with a standard error of about 0.25 fits Zeeuws and Soetens (2007) with 36 rather than 16 (editors' reading of the figure and calculation, approximate).

reporting_issues.issue: The methods call a fail-safe N large, making publication bias unlikely, only if it exceeds 5k + 10, with k the number of meta-analysed studies, and the publication-bias analyses used published reports only (p. 1076). The reported values are 39 for inhibitory control (22 published studies) and 59 for delayed memory (11 studies), both below that threshold (editors' arithmetic: 5 × 22 + 10 = 120 and 5 × 11 + 10 = 65; the short-term memory value of 2 is far below its threshold of 65). The text flags 39 with 'However' as fewer than two studies per published report, yet still treats the inhibitory-control estimate as most likely not affected by publication bias (p. 1077).
reporting_issues.consequence: For inhibitory control the robustness claim rests on funnel-plot symmetry and an unchanged trim-and-fill estimate, not on the fail-safe N; for delayed memory all three indicators point towards publication bias.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract names working memory and long-term memory as the effects qualified by publication bias and presents short-term episodic memory as a small but significant effect, but the results report that trim-and-fill reduced the short-term estimate to a non-significant 0.12 (−0.06 to 0.29) and that two null studies would nullify it.
reporting_issues.consequence: Three of the four pooled estimates, not two, are sensitive to publication-bias adjustment; only inhibitory control is robust to it.

reporting_issues.issue: The methods state that Hedges' correction factor J corrects the tendency of small studies to bias the mean effect upwards because of publication bias (p. 1074); J corrects the small-sample upward bias of Cohen's d and has nothing to do with publication bias.
reporting_issues.consequence: A misstatement of method; the numbers are unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: Tables 2, 3 and 5 give Ilieva et al. (2013) 50% men (editors' check against that trial's own report: 22 men among 46, 48%). The delayed-memory text gives the high-dose samples as 48% to 70% men (p. 1084), a lower bound that matches the trial's own 48% rather than Table 5, which lists 50%, 61.11% and 70% for three high-dose studies and does not report the fourth (p. 1083).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; it slightly affects the sex-ratio meta-regression input for one study, and the paper does not say which value entered the analysis.

reporting_issues.issue: The funnel plots, trim-and-fill and fail-safe N used published reports only and effect sizes without Hedges' correction (p. 1076), so the adjusted values are printed as d (pp. 1077, 1084–1085), while the text presents each as a reduction of the primary g, which also includes unpublished data; the unadjusted estimates for the published studies alone are not reported in numbers.
reporting_issues.consequence: Each reported reduction mixes the trim-and-fill adjustment with a change of study set and of metric, so its size is approximate; for delayed memory all 11 studies were published, so only the small-sample correction differs.
