design_detail: Retrospective cohort with an active comparator, restricted to people starting the drugs (incident use), in two US commercial insurance claims databases (Optum Clinformatics and IBM MarketScan). 337,919 people aged 13 to 25 years with an outpatient ADHD diagnosis who started methylphenidate (or dexmethylphenidate) or amphetamine (amphetamine-dextroamphetamine, dextroamphetamine or lisdexamfetamine) between 1 January 2004 and 30 September 2015; 1:1 propensity-score matching within each database (110,923 per group), Cox models, results pooled across the two databases by fixed-effect meta-analysis. Outcome: a new diagnosis code for psychosis with an antipsychotic prescription within 60 days.
can_establish: In commercially insured US 13- to 25-year-olds with ADHD who started a stimulant, how often a new psychotic episode treated with an antipsychotic was recorded during the first months of use, and whether it was recorded more often after starting amphetamine than methylphenidate among patients balanced on the characteristics that claims record.
cannot_establish: That amphetamine itself causes the difference (unrecorded substance use, prodromal symptoms, family history and prescriber choice may differ between the groups); risk at particular doses (no dose data) or whether the medicine was actually taken; risk over years (median follow-up 113 to 162 days); milder psychotic symptoms not treated with an antipsychotic; risk in people with public or no insurance, adults over 25, children under 13, or with non-prescribed use.

sample.recruitment: Insurance claims (registry-type data): Optum Clinformatics (United Healthcare members, data for 68 million patients) and IBM MarketScan (large employers and insurance plans, 185 million) (p. 1129).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: age 13 to 25 at entry; at least one outpatient encounter with an ADHD diagnosis (ICD-9 314); a new prescription of methylphenidate or amphetamine with no claim for either in the previous 12 months; 1 year of continuous medical and prescription enrolment. Excluded: unspecified psychosis, hallucinations, delusional disorder, schizophrenia-spectrum disorders, drug-induced psychoses, mood disorders with psychotic features, bipolar disorder, CNS disease or narcolepsy; mood stabilizers, antipsychotics or other stimulants (phentermine, pemoline, methamphetamine) in the previous 12 months; oral glucocorticoids in the previous 60 days; people who started both drugs (p. 1129; Figure 1, p. 1130).
sample.demographics: Matched groups (Table 1, p. 1134): mean age 17.0 (SD 3.1 to 3.2) in Optum and 17.1 in MarketScan; 37.2% to 37.5% female; depression 16.0% to 19.2%; anxiety or PTSD 11.2% to 13.0%; recorded alcohol use disorder 1.1% to 1.5%; recorded cannabis use disorder 1.0% to 1.4%; prescribers: family or internal medicine physicians 35.1% to 36.9%, paediatricians 28.2% to 34.8%, psychiatrists 17.7% to 21.3%. Race, ethnic group and socioeconomic status were not available (p. 1137).
sample.attrition: Follow-up began 7 days after the first dispensing and was censored at psychosis, stopping the stimulant (60 days after the end of supply), switching to the other stimulant, death, end of enrolment or 31 December 2016 (p. 1131); 864 and 1697 eligible patients never began follow-up (Figure 1, p. 1130). Median follow-up was longer with amphetamine: 155 vs 113 days in Optum and 162 vs 123 days in MarketScan; stopping the stimulant was the commonest reason for censoring; 13.8% of methylphenidate starters switched to amphetamine and 5.6% of amphetamine starters to methylphenidate (p. 1133).
sample.selection_effects: Commercially insured patients only; the authors state the results do not apply to people with public or no insurance, who are disproportionately Black or Hispanic (p. 1137). Older patients and patients of family or internal medicine physicians were more often prescribed amphetamine (p. 1133). Matching kept 92.7% of methylphenidate starters but 50.8% of amphetamine starters (editors' calculation from Figure 1), so the estimate describes amphetamine starters who resembled methylphenidate starters.

exposure.measurement: Outpatient pharmacy dispensing claims: the medicines were prescribed and dispensed, but whether or how they were taken is unknown (p. 1137).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Dose was not recorded or analysed. Formulation analyses: extended-release only, lisdexamfetamine against extended-release methylphenidate, and immediate-release (p. 1135). The exposure window extended to 60 days after the supply ended (Figure 2, p. 1131).
exposure.polysubstance: Recorded substance use disorders and other prescriptions (antidepressants, benzodiazepines, prescription opioids) were balanced by matching (Table 1); actual substance use is not captured in claims. The authors used negative-control outcomes (emergency or inpatient care for substance use disorders, and non-psychotic depression) and a bias analysis for unrecorded cannabis use (pp. 1133, 1135).

comparison.controls: Active comparator: people starting methylphenidate, matched 1:1 to people starting amphetamine within each database on a propensity score (maximum difference 1%) estimated from all prespecified covariates (p. 1132).
comparison.matching: Covariates over the previous 365 days: year and age at entry, sex, region, insurance type; markers of ADHD severity (outpatient ADHD visits, emergency or inpatient care with ADHD, non-stimulant ADHD medicines, oppositional-defiant or conduct disorder), asthma, other psychiatric disorders and medicines, substance use disorders, provider type and health-care use; maximal standardized mean difference after matching 0.02 (pp. 1132–1133; Table 1).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Unrecorded substance use, prodromal symptoms of psychosis, family history of psychosis, socioeconomic status, race and ethnic group, and ADHD severity beyond what claims show (pp. 1133, 1136–1137).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Recorded substance use disorders were balanced (alcohol 1.1% to 1.5%, cannabis 1.0% to 1.4%; Table 1); unrecorded use is unknown. From a national survey the authors estimated cannabis use at 35.8% among people with ADHD (p. 1135).

outcomes.instruments: Primary: an ICD-9 or ICD-10 code for a new inpatient or outpatient diagnosis of psychosis (unspecified psychosis, hallucinations, delusional disorder, other stimulant use disorders with psychosis, schizophrenia-spectrum disorders, major depressive or bipolar disorder with psychotic features) plus an antipsychotic prescription on the same day or within 60 days (p. 1131). Stricter definitions: one inpatient or two outpatient codes, or two inpatient or outpatient codes, each with an antipsychotic prescription (Table 2). Negative controls: emergency or inpatient care for alcohol, cannabis, opioid or all other substance use disorders, and major depression without psychotic features, at 100 days (p. 1133).
outcomes.validity_norms: Positive predictive value 93.1% in an external validation in an electronic health record database (p. 1131); 91.3% in an internal review of claims profiles by a psychiatrist unaware of the drug group, with 10.1% (methylphenidate) and 8.4% (amphetamine) of cases judged unlikely to be true psychosis (p. 1132); 96.7% and 98.2% for the two stricter definitions (Table 2).
outcomes.operationalization: Treated new-onset psychosis: psychosis serious enough to be coded and treated with an antipsychotic. Episodes in the first 7 days of use were excluded by design; a post hoc analysis counting from day 1 was reported as consistent (p. 1135).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. One prespecified primary outcome and estimand, five negative-control outcomes, and at least 13 further estimates (adjustment methods, stricter definitions, subgroups, formulations) in the main text; the subgroup analyses are labelled post hoc.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The reviewer of claims profiles was unaware of the drug group (p. 1131); the primary analysis was prespecified before unblinding of exposure status (Table 2, footnote, p. 1136).

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary (matched, pooled): 106 episodes (0.10%) among 110,923 methylphenidate starters and 237 (0.21%) among 110,923 amphetamine starters; hazard ratio 1.65 (95% CI 1.31 to 2.09); incidence 1.78 vs 2.83 per 1000 person-years; in all, 343 episodes in 143,286 person-years (2.4 per 1000) (pp. 1128, 1133; Table 2). Editors' calculations: rate difference 1.05 per 1000 person-years; rate ratio 1.59; 1 episode per 647 matched patients (1 per 616 in the full cohort). Full cohort: unadjusted 120 (0.10%) vs 429 (0.20%), HR 1.44 (1.17 to 1.77); multivariable-adjusted HR 1.55 (1.25 to 1.92). Stricter definitions (matched): 89 (0.08%) vs 211 (0.19%), HR 1.75 (1.36 to 2.25); 71 (0.06%) vs 163 (0.15%), HR 1.68 (1.26 to 2.22). Post hoc subgroups: 13 to 17 years 1.62 (1.24 to 2.12); 18 to 25 years 1.41 (0.99 to 2.00); family or internal medicine 1.78 (1.21 to 2.62); paediatricians 1.70 (1.09 to 2.67); psychiatrists 1.38 (0.93 to 2.04). Formulations: extended-release only 1.77 (1.30 to 2.40); lisdexamfetamine vs extended-release methylphenidate 1.54 (1.10 to 2.16); immediate-release 1.32 (0.77 to 2.29). Negative controls: alcohol 1.12 (0.95 to 1.33), other substances 1.10 (0.95 to 1.29), cannabis 1.12 (0.91 to 1.38), opioids 0.91 (0.63 to 1.33), non-psychotic depression 1.03 (0.84 to 1.27). Median time from first dispensing to the episode 128 days (IQR 48 to 333).
analysis.covariates: Primary: propensity-score matching. Secondary: multivariable Cox models in the full cohort adjusted for age and year at entry, sex, region, insurance type, smoking status, oppositional-defiant or conduct disorder, depression, anxiety, alcohol, cannabis and all other substance use disorders, non-stimulant ADHD medicines, antidepressants, benzodiazepines and prescription opioids, with provider type in some models (Table 2, footnote). Missing age, sex, region and insurance type (0.002% to 2.4%) handled with indicator variables; complete-case and multiple-imputation analyses did not change the results meaningfully (pp. 1132, 1135).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is reported. The primary matched and pooled hazard ratio was prespecified before unblinding of exposure status (Table 2, footnote); further sensitivity analyses are described as prespecified and the subgroup analyses as post hoc (p. 1132).
analysis.selective_reporting: Database-specific results, several prespecified sensitivity analyses (90-day risk window, 100-day maximum follow-up, confidence intervals allowing for 10% to 40% overlap between the databases, a 30-day antipsychotic window, one diagnosis plus two antipsychotic prescriptions) and the post hoc 365-day analysis by starting drug regardless of switching are reported only as consistent, with numbers in the Supplementary Appendix (Tables S5 to S9), which was not read.
analysis.power: At least 80% power to detect a 50% higher risk with amphetamine (p. 1132); the authors call the subgroup analyses underpowered (p. 1136).

interpretation_gap.results_show: A new psychotic episode treated with an antipsychotic was rare in both groups during the first months of use (0.10% vs 0.21% of matched patients; 1.78 vs 2.83 per 1000 person-years) and occurred at about 1.65 times the rate (hazard ratio) after starting amphetamine compared with methylphenidate, consistently across databases, adjustment methods and stricter outcome definitions; the absolute difference was about 1 episode per 1000 person-years.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract's conclusion that amphetamine use was associated with a greater risk fits the design. Gaps: (1) the closing statement that the risk was about twice as high with amphetamine (p. 1137) rests on the crude proportions (0.21% vs 0.10%), which are inflated by the amphetamine group's longer follow-up; the prespecified hazard ratio is 1.65 and the rate ratio 1.59 (editors' calculation). (2) Approximately 1 in 660 patients (abstract, p. 1128; p. 1137) is a proportion over a median of about 4 to 5 months of follow-up, not a yearly or lifetime risk, and the matched counts give 1 in 647 (editors' calculation). (3) The Results say the higher risk was not found among psychiatrists' patients (p. 1135) on the basis of an interval of 0.93 to 2.04, without an interaction test; the Discussion words it more cautiously as a lower effect size in a post hoc, underpowered analysis (p. 1136). (4) The Discussion's attribution of the higher risk to amphetamine, supported by negative-control outcomes (p. 1137), is reasonable, but three of those controls had point estimates of 1.10 to 1.12.

timeline.event: The US Food and Drug Administration required stimulant labels to warn of treatment-emergent psychotic or manic symptoms, after preapproval trials showed 11 patients with psychotic symptoms over 743 person-years (as summarized by Moran et al., p. 1129, citing Mosholder et al., 2009; not read)
This cohort: hazard ratio 1.65 for treated new psychosis after starting amphetamine compared with methylphenidate in 13- to 25-year-olds

replication.where_it_stands: No replication is among the papers read for this round, and the editors have not searched for one. The two network meta-analyses read with it (Cortese et al., 2018; Farhat et al., 2025) did not study psychosis. A single, large, carefully designed claims analysis: its relative estimate holds across the analyses shown, while its absolute numbers are small and apply to the first months of use.

what_would_settle_it: Because treated psychosis is rare (about 2 to 3 per 1000 person-years here), a randomized comparison large enough is unlikely; the next step is replication with the same design (people starting each drug, compared with each other) in other data (public insurance, other countries, adults over 25) with dose information, longer follow-up and validated outcomes, together with within-person designs comparing periods on and off each drug.

domains.note: Active-comparator design restricted to people starting each drug, with propensity-score matching on many claims variables (maximal standardized difference 0.02), a multivariable model giving a similar estimate (1.55), near-null negative controls and a bias analysis for cannabis (pp. 1133–1135). Unrecorded substance use, prodromal symptoms, family history and prescriber choice (amphetamine was prescribed more by family or internal medicine physicians and to older patients) can still confound; three substance-use negative controls had point estimates of 1.10 to 1.12.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: New starters only, with prior psychosis, bipolar disorder and antipsychotic or mood-stabilizer use excluded in both groups; follow-up started at the same point (day 7) in both, and a post hoc analysis from day 1 was reported as consistent (p. 1135).
Drug group defined from dispensing claims recorded before the outcome. Whether the medicine was taken is unknown (p. 1137), which would more likely blur than create a difference.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: As-treated analysis censored at stopping and switching; methylphenidate starters switched more often (13.8% vs 5.6%), and if switching followed early symptoms the censoring was informative. The post hoc analysis by starting drug over 365 days is reported as consistent, but its numbers are only in the supplement (pp. 1132, 1135).
Age, sex, region or insurance type missing for 0.002% to 2.4%; complete-case and multiple-imputation analyses did not change the results meaningfully (pp. 1132, 1135).

Validated outcome definition (positive predictive value 91.3% to 93.1%) checked by a reviewer unaware of the drug group, with similar proportions of unlikely cases in both groups (10.1% vs 8.4%); stricter definitions gave similar hazard ratios (1.75 and 1.68). Whether contact with care, and so the chance of detection, differed by drug is not examined.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Primary analysis prespecified before unblinding of exposure; unadjusted, adjusted and matched estimates are all reported (Table 2); several sensitivity results are given only in the supplement.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I is used because the study compares two treatments given in practice (interventions) without randomization. The overall judgment, moderate, follows the confounding and deviation domains: the design is about as strong as claims data allow, but unrecorded substance use, prodromal symptoms and prescriber choice cannot be excluded, and censoring at switching may not be random. Cite for: in commercially insured US 13- to 25-year-olds starting a prescribed stimulant for ADHD, about 1 in 650 had a new psychotic episode treated with an antipsychotic during a median follow-up of 4 to 5 months, and the rate was higher after starting amphetamine than methylphenidate (HR 1.65, 1.31 to 2.09; 2.83 vs 1.78 per 1000 person-years). Do not cite for: risk with non-prescribed use, at particular doses, over years, in older adults or with public insurance, or as proof that amphetamine itself causes the difference.

key_findings.finding: 337,919 people aged 13 to 25 started a stimulant for ADHD (232,096 person-years of follow-up): 119,708 methylphenidate and 218,211 amphetamine. After 1:1 propensity-score matching there were 110,923 per group (221,846 in all; 143,286 person-years), with maximal standardized mean differences of 0.02.
key_findings.locator: Results › Patients, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 (p. 1130)

key_findings.finding: Primary analysis: 106 treated psychotic episodes (0.10%) among 110,923 methylphenidate starters and 237 (0.21%) among 110,923 amphetamine starters; pooled hazard ratio 1.65 (95% CI 1.31 to 2.09); incidence 1.78 vs 2.83 episodes per 1000 person-years of drug exposure.
key_findings.locator: Results › Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (p. 1136)

key_findings.finding: Absolute numbers: 343 episodes in 143,286 person-years in the matched population, 2.4 per 1000 person-years, which the authors summarize as approximately 1 in 660 patients; they put the difference between the drugs at about 1 per 1000 person-years. Editors' calculation: 343 of 221,846 is 1 in 647; the rate difference is 1.05 per 1000 person-years.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results and Conclusions (p. 1128); Discussion, 5th and 6th paragraphs (p. 1137)

key_findings.finding: In the full, unmatched cohort there were 120 episodes (0.10%) among methylphenidate starters and 429 (0.20%) among amphetamine starters: unadjusted HR 1.44 (1.17 to 1.77); multivariable-adjusted HR 1.55 (1.25 to 1.92).
key_findings.locator: Table 2, Primary analysis rows

key_findings.finding: Stricter outcome definitions gave similar results: one inpatient or two outpatient psychosis codes with an antipsychotic (positive predictive value 96.7%), 89 (0.08%) vs 211 (0.19%), HR 1.75 (1.36 to 2.25); two inpatient or outpatient codes with an antipsychotic (98.2%), 71 (0.06%) vs 163 (0.15%), HR 1.68 (1.26 to 2.22).
key_findings.locator: Table 2, Sensitivity analyses rows

key_findings.finding: The median time from the first stimulant dispensing to the psychotic episode was 128 days (IQR 48 to 333). Median follow-up was 155 days (IQR 82 to 318) with amphetamine vs 113 (82 to 209) with methylphenidate in Optum, and 162 (82 to 339) vs 123 (82 to 228) in MarketScan.
key_findings.locator: Results › Patients, 1st paragraph; Results › Outcomes, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Switching: 16,489 of 119,708 methylphenidate starters (13.8%) switched to amphetamine and 12,233 of 218,211 amphetamine starters (5.6%) switched to methylphenidate; follow-up was censored at switching.
key_findings.locator: Results › Patients, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Post hoc subgroups: 13 to 17 years HR 1.62 (1.24 to 2.12), with 82 (0.11%) vs 181 (0.21%) episodes; 18 to 25 years 1.41 (0.99 to 2.00), 38 (0.09%) vs 248 (0.19%); patients of family or internal medicine physicians 1.78 (1.21 to 2.62); paediatricians 1.70 (1.09 to 2.67); psychiatrists 1.38 (0.93 to 2.04), whose patients had the highest proportions in both groups (0.17% vs 0.29%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Additional Analyses, 1st paragraph (p. 1135); Table 2, Subgroup analyses rows (p. 1136)

key_findings.finding: By formulation: extended-release only HR 1.77 (1.30 to 2.40); lisdexamfetamine against extended-release methylphenidate 1.54 (1.10 to 2.16); immediate-release 1.32 (0.77 to 2.29).
key_findings.locator: Results › Additional Analyses, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Negative-control outcomes (emergency or inpatient care, at 100 days) did not differ between the groups: alcohol use disorder HR 1.12 (0.95 to 1.33; 929 events), all other substance use disorders 1.10 (0.95 to 1.29; 1062), cannabis use disorder 1.12 (0.91 to 1.38; 542), opioid use disorder 0.91 (0.63 to 1.33; 228), depression without psychotic features 1.03 (0.84 to 1.27; 491).
key_findings.locator: Results › Additional Analyses, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Bias analysis: with cannabis use estimated at 35.8% among people with ADHD (national survey) and an assumed relative risk of psychosis of 2.0 with any cannabis use, cannabis use among amphetamine starters would have to be 97.0% to explain the finding, a difference of 61 percentage points.
key_findings.locator: Results › Additional Analyses, 2nd paragraph (p. 1135); Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 1137)

key_findings.finding: Outcome validation: positive predictive value 93.1% in an external health-record database and 91.3% in an internal review of claims profiles by a psychiatrist unaware of the drug group; cases judged unlikely to be true psychosis were 10.1% with methylphenidate and 8.4% with amphetamine.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Outcomes, 1st paragraph (p. 1131) and 2nd paragraph (p. 1131, continuing on p. 1132)

key_findings.finding: Amphetamine was prescribed to 72.5% of the patients of family or internal medicine physicians, 51.6% of paediatricians' patients and 63.7% of psychiatrists' patients; 3.8 times as many patients received a prescription for amphetamine in 2014 as in 2005, against 1.6 times as many for methylphenidate.
key_findings.locator: Results › Patients, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Recorded substance use disorders were uncommon and balanced after matching: alcohol use disorder 1.4% vs 1.5% (Optum) and 1.1% vs 1.1% (MarketScan); cannabis use disorder 1.4% vs 1.4% and 1.0% vs 1.0%.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Substance use rows

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: unmeasured confounders such as under-reported substance use disorders; possible misuse and diversion (reported diversion 18.6% to 61.7% among people with stimulant prescriptions, greater for amphetamine); no knowledge of whether or how the medicines were taken; no data on race, ethnic group or socioeconomic status; results not generalizable to public or no insurance. They argue that misuse would predict larger effects in college-age patients and with immediate-release forms, where the effects were smaller.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The closing statement that the risk was about twice as high with amphetamine (Discussion, 6th paragraph) does not match the prespecified pooled hazard ratio of 1.65 (1.31 to 2.09); a factor of about 2 matches only the crude proportions (0.21% vs 0.10%), which do not allow for the amphetamine group's longer follow-up. Editors' calculation: the incidence rates (2.83 vs 1.78 per 1000 person-years) give a ratio of 1.59.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should give the hazard ratio (1.65) or the two rates rather than a doubling.

reporting_issues.issue: Approximately 1 in 660 patients (abstract; Discussion, 6th paragraph) does not match the counts. Editors' arithmetic: 343 of 221,846 matched patients is 1 in 647, and 549 of 337,919 in the full cohort is 1 in 616.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the figure is in any case a proportion over a few months of follow-up, not a yearly or lifetime risk.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2 the amphetamine age subgroups (86,505 and 131,693) add up to 13 patients fewer than the full amphetamine cohort (218,211), while their episodes add up (181 and 248, 429 in all) (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Trivial; possibly patients with missing age.

reporting_issues.issue: The subgroup rows of Table 2 give full-cohort, unmatched patient counts, and the method behind their hazard ratios is indicated only by a footnote on multivariable models; no test of interaction between subgroups is reported, although the Results state there was no higher risk among psychiatrists' patients (HR 1.38, 0.93 to 2.04).
reporting_issues.consequence: Differences between subgroups (age, prescriber) are not demonstrated and should not be presented as findings.
